LeBron James.text: His high school games were sold on pay-per-view to Ohio cable subscribers, at $7.95 a game.
LeBron James.evidence: Time Warner Cable, looking to capitalize on James's popularity, offered St. Vincent–St. Mary's games to Ohio-based subscribers for $7.95 per game on a pay-per-view basis throughout the season, but this ended up not being profitable.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.text: College basketball banned the dunk to curb his dominance, a move dubbed the "Alcindor Rule" after his birth name.
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.evidence: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (born Ferdinand Lewis Alcindor Jr.; April 16, 1947) is an American former professional basketball player. ... After the season, the dunk was banned in college basketball in an attempt to curtail his dominance; critics dubbed it the "Alcindor Rule".

Karl Malone.text: He was so sure Dallas would draft him that he had already rented an apartment there; Utah took him 13th.
Karl Malone.evidence: In the 1985 NBA draft, the Utah Jazz selected Karl Malone with the 13th overall pick. ... In fact, Malone was so convinced the Dallas Mavericks were going to select him with the eighth choice that he had already rented an apartment in Dallas.

Kobe Bryant.text: He was named after Kobe beef his father saw on a menu; his middle name, Bean, is from his dad's nickname "Jellybean".
Kobe Bryant.evidence: His father named him after the Kobe beef from Japan, which he saw on a restaurant menu, whereas his middle name, Bean, was derived from his father's nickname "Jellybean".

Kevin Durant.text: He took number 35 in honor of his childhood AAU coach, who was murdered at the age of 35.
Kevin Durant.evidence: During this time, he began wearing #35 as his jersey number in honor of his AAU coach, Charles Craig, who was murdered at the age of 35.

Michael Jordan.text: At North Carolina he was interested in becoming a meteorologist, so he majored in cultural geography.
Michael Jordan.evidence: In 1980 he accepted a basketball scholarship to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He was interested in becoming a meteorologist, and majored in cultural geography because of its relationship to meteorology.

Dirk Nowitzki.text: As a struggling rookie he was heckled as "Irk Nowitzki", minus the D because it stands for defense.
Dirk Nowitzki.evidence: Played as a power forward by coach Don Nelson, the 20-year-old felt overpowered by the more athletic NBA forwards, was intimidated by the expectations as a number nine pick, and played bad defense; hecklers taunted him as "Irk Nowitzki", omitting the "D" which stands for "defense" in basketball slang.

Wilt Chamberlain.text: As a teen he beat college star B. H. Born 25-10 one-on-one; Born dropped his NBA plans and became a tractor engineer.
Wilt Chamberlain.evidence: Auerbach spotted Chamberlain playing there and had him play one-on-one against University of Kansas (KU) standout and national champion B. H. Born, elected NCAA Most Outstanding Player in 1953. Chamberlain won 25–10; Born was so dejected he gave up a promising NBA career and became a tractor engineer; according to Born, "If there were high school kids that good, I figured I wasn't going to make it to the pros".

James Harden.text: His mother nicknamed him "Lucky": he came after a string of miscarriages, ten years after his siblings.
James Harden.evidence: Before his birth, after that of his older sister, their mother suffered a string of miscarriages. With a 10 year age gap between Harden and his older siblings, she nicknamed him “Lucky”.

Shaquille O'Neal.text: He missed being the first unanimous MVP by one vote, cast by CNN's Fred Hickman for Allen Iverson.
Shaquille O'Neal.evidence: O'Neal was also voted the 1999–2000 regular season Most Valuable Player, one vote short of becoming the first unanimous MVP in NBA history. Fred Hickman, then of CNN, instead chose Allen Iverson, then of the Philadelphia 76ers, who went on to win MVP the next season.
